q: The stomach wall has a lining that secretes mucus, layers that contract to churn food, nerves that coordinate the contractions, and a layer that binds these together. Which statement explains why the stomach is classified at the organ level?
o: It works with the esophagus and intestines to digest food
Its wall combines two or more tissue types working together
It contains several cell types, all within its mucus lining
Its lining cells are specialized to secrete mucus and acid
w: The mucus-secreting lining is epithelial tissue, the contracting layers are muscle tissue, the nerves are nervous tissue and the binding layer is connective tissue. Two or more tissue types working together make an organ, and the stomach has all four.

n.0: Cooperating with other organs is what places the stomach in an organ system (the digestive system); it does not explain why the stomach itself is an organ.
n.2: Several cell types within one layer can still be a single tissue, as in blood. An organ needs two or more tissue types.
n.3: Specialized cells describe the cellular or tissue level. Specialization alone does not make a structure an organ.

q: A biology quiz pairs four structures with levels of organization. Which pairing correctly matches the structure with the level of organization it represents?
o: A single neuron with the tissue level
Cardiac muscle tissue with the organ level
A kidney with the organ system level
A glucose molecule with the chemical level
w: Atoms and molecules such as glucose make up the chemical level, the simplest level of organization.

n.0: A single neuron is one cell, so it belongs at the cellular level. Nervous tissue is the tissue-level structure.
n.1: Cardiac muscle is a tissue. The heart, which contains cardiac muscle plus other tissues, is the organ.
n.2: A kidney is one organ. The kidneys, ureters, bladder and urethra together form the urinary system.

q: A patient education leaflet groups the kidneys, ureters, urinary bladder and urethra together because they work as a unit to remove wastes in urine. Which level of organization does this grouping represent?
o: Tissue, because the structures are lined by similar epithelial cells
Organ, because each structure contains two or more tissue types
Organ system, because several organs cooperate in one function
Organism, because removing wastes keeps the whole body alive
w: Each structure listed is an organ. A group of organs that cooperate to carry out one major function is an organ system, here the urinary system.

n.0: A shared epithelial lining is one tissue within each organ. The leaflet groups whole organs, not a tissue.
n.1: That reasoning describes each structure on its own. The question asks about the group, and a group of cooperating organs is an organ system.
n.3: The organism level is the whole person made of all organ systems together, not a single system.

q: A medication works by binding to a receptor protein on the surface of liver cells. At which level of organization does the receptor protein itself belong?
o: Chemical, because a protein is a large molecule built from atoms
Cellular, because it sits on the plasma membrane of a cell
Tissue, because liver cells form a group with a shared function
Organ, because its effects change how the whole liver functions
w: A protein is a molecule, and atoms and molecules make up the chemical level. Its location on a cell does not change its own level.

n.1: The receptor is part of a cell, but a part of a cell is not a cell. The protein is a molecule at the chemical level.
n.2: The liver cells together form a tissue, but the receptor protein on one cell is a molecule.
n.3: The drug's effect reaches the organ, but the receptor protein itself is a molecule at the chemical level.

q: A student argues that a single cardiac muscle cell taken from the heart should be classified at the tissue level. Which statement best explains why this classification is incorrect?
o: A muscle cell belongs at the chemical level because it is made of proteins
A tissue is a group of similar cells working together, and this is a single cell
A tissue requires an extracellular matrix of fibers, which one muscle cell lacks
A tissue must be supplied by blood vessels, and a single muscle cell has none
w: A tissue is a group of similar cells that work together. One cell on its own, even a highly specialized one, is classified at the cellular level.

n.0: Proteins are at the chemical level, but a whole living cell built from them is at the cellular level.
n.2: An abundant extracellular matrix is a feature of connective tissue. Epithelial and muscle tissues have very little matrix between their cells, yet they are still tissues.
n.3: Epithelium is a tissue but is avascular, so blood vessels are not what makes something a tissue.

q: Which sequence names a structure at each of three successive levels of organization, listed from the lowest of the three levels to the highest?
o: Stomach, digestive system, small intestine
Epithelial cell, epithelial tissue, stomach
Protein, epithelial tissue, epithelial cell
Muscle cell, the heart, cardiac muscle tissue
w: An epithelial cell is the cellular level, epithelial tissue is the tissue level, and the stomach (built from four tissue types) is the organ level: three successive levels in rising order.

n.0: This runs organ, organ system, organ. The small intestine is another organ, so the sequence drops back a level.
n.2: This runs chemical, tissue, cellular. The cell must come before the tissue.
n.3: This runs cell, organ, tissue. The tissue level must come before the organ level.

q: The pleura, the serous pericardium and the peritoneum belong to one membrane type. Which choice names that type and correctly places its visceral layer?
o: Serous membrane; visceral layer on the wall
Serous membrane; visceral layer on the organ
Synovial membrane; visceral layer on the wall
Mucous membrane; visceral layer on the organ
w: The pleura, serous pericardium and peritoneum are serous membranes, which line closed body cavities. Each has a parietal layer on the cavity wall and a visceral layer on the surface of the organ, with serous fluid between them to reduce friction.

n.0: The membrane type is right, but the layers are reversed: the parietal layer lines the wall and the visceral layer covers the organ.
n.2: Synovial membranes line the cavities of freely movable joints, and in a serous membrane the visceral layer covers the organ, not the wall.
n.3: Mucous membranes line tracts that open to the outside (digestive, respiratory, urinary, reproductive); the pleura and peritoneum line closed cavities.

q: A histology student is comparing the four basic tissue types. Which feature distinguishes connective tissue from epithelial, muscle and nervous tissue?
o: Cells that generate and conduct electrical impulses
Cells scattered within an extracellular matrix of fibers
Cells joined tightly together with an exposed free surface
Cells that shorten when stimulated to produce movement
w: Connective tissue cells are scattered within an extracellular matrix made of ground substance and fibers (collagen, elastic, reticular). In blood, the matrix is fluid plasma.

n.0: Generating and conducting impulses describes the neurons of nervous tissue.
n.2: Tightly joined cells with a free (apical) surface describe epithelial tissue.
n.3: Contractility describes muscle tissue.

q: A classmate claims that epithelial tissue and every kind of connective tissue are supplied directly by blood vessels. Which correction is accurate?
o: Bone and blood are avascular and are nourished by diffusion
Cartilage is vascular, but epithelium is nourished by diffusion
Epithelium and cartilage are both avascular and fed by diffusion
Epithelium is vascular, but cartilage is nourished by diffusion
w: Epithelial tissue is avascular and is fed by diffusion from underlying connective tissue. Most connective tissue is vascular, but cartilage is an avascular exception.

n.0: Bone is a vascular connective tissue, and blood flows inside vessels as the fluid connective tissue.
n.1: Cartilage is the avascular connective tissue; this option reverses the facts for both tissues.
n.3: Epithelium has no blood vessels between its cells; it relies on diffusion from the tissue below.

q: Which pair names, in order, the membrane lining the nasal cavity and the membrane lining the cavity of the knee joint?
o: Serous membrane; synovial membrane
Cutaneous membrane; serous membrane
Mucous membrane; synovial membrane
Mucous membrane; serous membrane
w: The nasal cavity opens to the outside, so it is lined by a mucous membrane, an epithelium that secretes mucus. Freely movable joints such as the knee are lined by a synovial membrane, which secretes lubricating synovial fluid.

n.0: The knee is correctly synovial, but serous membranes line closed body cavities such as the pleural cavity, not the open nasal passage.
n.1: The cutaneous membrane is the skin, and the knee joint cavity is lined by synovial membrane, not serous membrane.
n.3: The nasal lining is correctly mucous, but serous membranes line closed body cavities; joint cavities are lined by synovial membrane.

q: A slide of tissue from a gland duct shows a single layer of cells that are about as tall as they are wide, each resting on the basement membrane. Which name fits this tissue?
o: Pseudostratified columnar epithelium
Simple cuboidal epithelium
Simple columnar epithelium
Stratified cuboidal epithelium
w: Epithelium is named by layers and cell shape. One layer is "simple," and cells about as tall as they are wide are "cuboidal," giving simple cuboidal epithelium.

n.0: Pseudostratified epithelium has tall cells with nuclei at different heights that look layered; these cells are cube-shaped.
n.2: Columnar cells are taller than they are wide; these cells are about equal in height and width.
n.3: "Stratified" means two or more layers; the sample has one layer.

q: The lining of the urinary bladder must stretch as the bladder fills and then return to its resting shape as it empties. Which tissue lines the bladder?
o: Transitional epithelium
Stratified squamous epithelium
Simple columnar epithelium
Dense regular connective tissue
w: Transitional epithelium is a stretchable epithelium whose cells change shape as the organ fills and empties. It lines the urinary bladder.

n.1: Stratified squamous epithelium is layered and protective (as in the epidermis) but is not the stretchable bladder lining.
n.2: Simple columnar epithelium is a single layer of tall cells, as in the lining of the GI tract; it does not stretch like the bladder lining.
n.3: Dense regular connective tissue forms tendons and ligaments; it is not a lining tissue.

q: In a tissue lining an airway, the nuclei sit at several different heights so the tissue looks layered, yet every cell touches the basement membrane. How should this tissue be classified?
o: Stratified, because the nuclei form two or more rows
Transitional, because its cells vary in height and shape
Pseudostratified, a single layer that only looks layered
Simple cuboidal, because each cell rests on the membrane
w: Pseudostratified epithelium is one layer of cells (every cell touches the basement membrane) whose nuclei sit at different heights, so it looks stratified.

n.0: Stratified epithelium has two or more true layers, with upper cells that do not touch the basement membrane.
n.1: Transitional epithelium is the stretchable lining of the bladder; uneven nuclei in one layer describe pseudostratified tissue.
n.3: Simple cuboidal cells are cube-shaped with nuclei in one row; nuclei at different heights point to pseudostratified epithelium.

q: The pancreas releases digestive enzymes through a duct into the small intestine and also releases insulin directly into the bloodstream. Which classification of the pancreas is correct?
o: An endocrine gland, because its enzymes act as hormones in the blood
Both an exocrine and an endocrine gland, with ducted and ductless parts
An exocrine gland, because insulin also leaves the gland through a duct
An endocrine gland, because a gland making any hormone is endocrine
w: Exocrine glands secrete through ducts onto a surface (the pancreatic enzymes), and endocrine glands are ductless and secrete hormones into the blood (insulin). The pancreas does both.

n.0: Digestive enzymes travel through a duct to the small intestine; they are exocrine secretions, not hormones.
n.2: Insulin is a hormone released directly into the blood without a duct, which is an endocrine function.
n.3: Making a hormone shows endocrine function, but the pancreas also secretes enzymes through a duct, so it is exocrine as well.

q: Tendons attach skeletal muscles to bones and must resist strong pulling forces in one direction. Which tissue forms tendons?
o: Dense irregular connective tissue
Loose areolar connective tissue
Dense regular connective tissue
Skeletal muscle tissue
w: Tendons and ligaments are dense regular connective tissue: tightly packed collagen fibers run parallel to one another, resisting strong pull in one direction.

n.0: Dense irregular connective tissue has collagen fibers running in many directions, suited to pull from several directions (as in the dermis), not the parallel fibers of a tendon.
n.1: Areolar tissue is loose connective tissue with a loose, open arrangement of fibers; it does not withstand strong one-direction pull.
n.3: Skeletal muscle generates the pull; the tendon that transmits it to bone is connective tissue.

q: Nervous tissue contains two main categories of cells: neurons and neuroglia. Which statement correctly describes the role of neuroglia?
o: They relay impulses between sensory and motor neurons in the CNS
They carry impulses from receptors toward the brain and spinal cord
They support, insulate and protect neurons but do not conduct impulses
They carry commands from the CNS out to muscles and glands
w: Neuroglia (glial cells) such as astrocytes, oligodendrocytes and Schwann cells support, nourish, insulate (myelin) and protect neurons. Conducting impulses is the job of the neurons themselves.

n.0: Relaying impulses between sensory and motor neurons is the role of interneurons, which are neurons.
n.1: Carrying impulses toward the CNS is the role of sensory (afferent) neurons.
n.3: Carrying commands from the CNS to effectors is the role of motor (efferent) neurons.

q: A patient has equal-sized scrapes to the outer layer of the skin and to the cartilage of the outer ear. Which prediction about healing is best supported?
o: Both heal at the same rate, because both tissues lack blood vessels
The cartilage heals first, because its matrix is supplied by capillaries
The skin heals first, because epithelium regenerates and cartilage is avascular
The cartilage heals first, because connective tissue is the most abundant tissue
w: Two facts combine. Epithelium (the outer layer of skin) has a high capacity for regeneration. Cartilage is an avascular connective tissue, so nutrients reach it slowly by diffusion and repair is slow. The skin heals first.

n.0: Both are avascular, but epithelium regenerates quickly while cartilage does not, so the rates differ.
n.1: Cartilage is avascular; its matrix has no capillaries, which is why it heals slowly.
n.3: How abundant a tissue type is in the body does not determine how fast a small injury heals.

q: Directional terms in anatomy are defined relative to anatomical position. Which description matches anatomical position?
o: Lying face up, arms at the sides, palms facing up, feet pointing forward
Standing upright, facing forward, arms at the sides, palms facing forward
Standing upright, facing forward, arms raised, palms facing forward
Standing upright, facing forward, arms at the sides, palms facing the thighs
w: In anatomical position the body is upright and facing forward, feet flat and pointing forward, arms at the sides, palms facing forward (anterior) with the thumbs pointing away from the body.

n.0: Lying face up is the supine position. Anatomical position is upright.
n.2: The arms hang at the sides in anatomical position; they are not raised.
n.3: Palms facing the thighs is a relaxed standing posture. In anatomical position the palms face forward.

q: The radius and ulna are the two bones of the forearm. In anatomical position, which term describes the location of the radius relative to the ulna?
o: Posterior
Lateral
Proximal
Medial
w: In anatomical position the palms face forward, so the radius (on the thumb side) lies farther from the midline than the ulna. The radius is lateral to the ulna.

n.0: With the palms facing forward, the two bones lie side by side, not one behind the other.
n.2: Proximal and distal compare distance from the limb's attachment. The radius and ulna lie side by side along the same length of forearm.
n.3: The ulna (little-finger side) is the medial bone; the radius is lateral to it.

q: A charting guide lists four example sentences that use proximal or distal. Which sentence uses one of these terms correctly?
o: The fingers are proximal to the palm
The knee is proximal to the ankle
The wrist is proximal to the elbow
The heart is distal to the stomach
w: Proximal means closer to where a limb attaches to the trunk. The knee is closer to the hip than the ankle is, so the knee is proximal to the ankle.

n.0: The fingers are farther from the limb's attachment than the palm, so they are distal to the palm.
n.2: The wrist is farther from the shoulder than the elbow is, so the wrist is distal to the elbow.
n.3: Proximal and distal describe limbs and branching structures. Organs of the trunk are compared with superior/inferior or anterior/posterior.

q: In anatomical position, which choice correctly describes both the forearm bones and the leg bones?
o: Radius lateral to ulna; tibia medial to fibula
Radius medial to ulna; tibia medial to fibula
Radius lateral to ulna; tibia lateral to fibula
Radius medial to ulna; tibia lateral to fibula
w: In anatomical position the palms face forward, so the radius (thumb side) is lateral to the ulna. In the leg, the large weight-bearing tibia is on the medial (big-toe) side and the slender fibula is lateral.

n.1: The tibia is correctly medial, but with the palms forward the radius lies on the thumb side, lateral to the ulna.
n.2: The radius is correctly lateral, but the tibia lies on the big-toe side, medial to the fibula.
n.3: Both halves are reversed: the radius is lateral to the ulna and the tibia is medial to the fibula.

q: A patient is lying face down on an exam table, and a nurse notes a bruise on the back of the right thigh, the surface facing the ceiling. Which term correctly describes the bruised surface of the thigh?
o: Lateral, because that surface faces away from the exam table
Superior, because the bruise faces upward while the patient lies prone
Anterior, because the bruise is on the surface farthest from the table
Posterior, because terms are based on anatomical position
w: Directional terms are defined by anatomical position no matter how the patient is lying. The back of the thigh is posterior.

n.0: Lateral means away from the midline of the body, not away from a table. The back of the thigh is its posterior surface.
n.1: Superior means toward the head in anatomical position, not toward the ceiling in the patient's current position.
n.2: Anterior is the front of the body. The back of the thigh stays posterior when the patient lies face down.

q: A nurse gives an intramuscular injection into the deltoid muscle of the upper arm. Which statement about the layers at the injection site uses superficial or deep correctly?
o: The hypodermis is superficial to the dermis
The epidermis is deep to the dermis
The deltoid muscle is deep to the hypodermis
The deltoid muscle is superficial to the dermis
w: From the surface inward the needle passes the epidermis, the dermis, the hypodermis (subcutaneous layer) and then the muscle. Deep means farther from the body surface, so the deltoid is deep to the hypodermis.

n.0: The hypodermis (subcutaneous layer) lies beneath the dermis, so it is deep to the dermis.
n.1: The epidermis is the outermost layer, so it is superficial to the dermis.
n.3: The deltoid lies beneath both the dermis and the hypodermis, so it is deep to the dermis.

q: Using the abdominal quadrants, which term describes the position of the sigmoid colon relative to the spleen?
o: Ipsilateral
Bilateral
Superior
Contralateral
w: The spleen is in the left upper quadrant and the sigmoid colon is in the left lower quadrant. Both lie on the patient's left side, and ipsilateral means on the same side of the body.

n.1: Bilateral describes paired structures found on both sides, such as the kidneys; it does not compare two unpaired organs.
n.2: The sigmoid colon is in a lower quadrant and the spleen in an upper one, so the sigmoid colon is inferior to the spleen.
n.3: Contralateral means on opposite sides. It would fit only if the spleen or the sigmoid colon were on the right, a common quadrant mistake.

q: The diaphragm forms the floor of the thoracic cavity. Which statement correctly describes its position in anatomical position?
o: It is superior to the lungs and inferior to the stomach
It is inferior to the heart and superior to the liver
It is inferior to the stomach and superior to the bladder
It is superior to the heart and inferior to the trachea
w: The diaphragm separates the thoracic cavity (heart, lungs) from the abdominopelvic cavity (liver, stomach). It lies below the heart and above the liver.

n.0: The lungs sit above the diaphragm and the stomach below it, so the diaphragm is inferior to the lungs and superior to the stomach.
n.2: The stomach lies below the diaphragm in the abdominal cavity, so the diaphragm is superior to the stomach.
n.3: The heart rests on the diaphragm, so the diaphragm is inferior to the heart.

q: A cut lies on the forearm, midway between the elbow and the wrist, on the thumb side. Using anatomical position, which description of the cut is accurate?
o: Proximal to the wrist, on the medial side of the forearm
Proximal to the wrist, on the lateral side of the forearm
Distal to the elbow, on the medial side of the forearm
Distal to the wrist, on the lateral side of the forearm
w: Two judgments are needed. The cut is closer to the shoulder than the wrist is, so it is proximal to the wrist. With palms facing forward, the thumb side is lateral.

n.0: Proximal to the wrist is right, but in anatomical position the thumb side is lateral, not medial.
n.2: Distal to the elbow is right, but the thumb side is lateral, not medial.
n.3: The cut is between the elbow and the wrist, so it is proximal to the wrist, not distal.

q: A post-surgical note states that a patient's incision lies caudal to the umbilicus, on the patient's right side. Which organ lies in the same abdominal quadrant as the incision?
o: The gallbladder
The appendix
The spleen
The sigmoid colon
w: Caudal is a synonym of inferior (toward the feet), so the incision is below the navel on the patient's right: the right lower quadrant, which contains the appendix and cecum.

n.0: The gallbladder is in the right upper quadrant. Choosing it treats caudal as if it meant cranial (toward the head).
n.2: The spleen is in the left upper quadrant, which is cranial to the navel and on the patient's left.
n.3: The sigmoid colon is below the navel but in the left lower quadrant, on the patient's left side.

q: A cut runs vertically from front to back through the nasal septum, the sternum and the umbilicus. Which plane is this, and what does it produce?
o: Midsagittal plane; equal left and right halves
Transverse plane; superior and inferior parts
Frontal plane; anterior and posterior parts
Parasagittal plane; unequal left and right parts
w: The nasal septum, sternum and umbilicus all lie on the midline, so a vertical front-to-back cut through all three is the midsagittal (median) plane, which divides the body into equal left and right halves.

n.1: A transverse plane is horizontal and separates upper from lower parts; this cut is vertical.
n.2: A frontal (coronal) plane runs from side to side and separates front from back; a front-to-back cut is a sagittal plane.
n.3: A parasagittal plane is vertical and runs front to back but lies off the midline; the nasal septum, sternum and umbilicus are midline structures.

q: A model of the human body is cut along a vertical plane that separates the face and chest from the back of the head and the back. Which plane was used?
o: Frontal (coronal) plane
Transverse (horizontal) plane
Midsagittal (median) plane
Parasagittal plane
w: The frontal (coronal) plane is vertical and divides the body into anterior (front) and posterior (back) portions.

n.1: The transverse plane is horizontal and divides superior from inferior.
n.2: The midsagittal plane divides the body into left and right halves, not front and back.
n.3: A parasagittal plane divides the body into unequal left and right parts.

q: The ventral body cavity is subdivided by a dome-shaped muscle that contracts during breathing. Which two cavities does the diaphragm separate?
o: The pleural and pericardial cavities
The abdominal and pelvic cavities
The cranial and vertebral (spinal) cavities
The thoracic and abdominopelvic cavities
w: The diaphragm separates the thoracic cavity (lungs, heart) above from the abdominopelvic cavity below.

n.0: The pleural and pericardial cavities both lie within the thoracic cavity above the diaphragm.
n.1: The abdominal and pelvic cavities are continuous, both within the abdominopelvic cavity below the diaphragm.
n.2: The cranial and vertebral cavities form the dorsal cavity; the diaphragm is part of the ventral cavity.

q: A diagram shows a patient facing the viewer, and an instructor points to the lower abdominal quadrant on the viewer's left side. Which organ is located in that quadrant?
o: The spleen
The appendix
The gallbladder
The sigmoid colon
w: Two steps: a patient facing the viewer has their right side on the viewer's left, so the instructor is pointing to the patient's right lower quadrant (RLQ), which contains the appendix and cecum.

n.0: The spleen is in the left upper quadrant, not a lower quadrant.
n.2: The gallbladder is in the right upper quadrant, under the liver, not a lower quadrant.
n.3: The sigmoid colon is in the left lower quadrant. That is the patient's left, which appears on the viewer's right.

q: The mediastinum is the central region of the thoracic cavity between the two lungs. Which structure is found in the mediastinum?
o: The spinal cord
The left lung
The esophagus
The right pleural cavity
w: The mediastinum contains the heart within its pericardial cavity, the trachea, the esophagus, the thymus and the great vessels.

n.0: The spinal cord is in the vertebral cavity, part of the dorsal cavity, not the ventral thoracic cavity.
n.1: Each lung lies in its own pleural cavity on either side of the mediastinum.
n.3: The pleural cavities flank the mediastinum; they surround the lungs.

q: Serous membranes reduce friction around organs in the ventral cavity. Which layer adheres directly to the outer surface of each lung?
o: Visceral pleura
Parietal peritoneum
Parietal pleura
Visceral pericardium
w: Serous membranes have a parietal layer lining the cavity wall and a visceral layer covering the organ. The pleura surrounds the lungs, so the layer on the lung surface is the visceral pleura.

n.1: The parietal peritoneum lines the wall of the abdominopelvic cavity.
n.2: The parietal pleura lines the wall of the thoracic cavity, not the lung surface.
n.3: The visceral pericardium covers the heart, not the lungs.

q: During a lumbar puncture, a needle is inserted between two lumbar vertebrae into the fluid-filled space of the vertebral canal. Which body cavity, and its larger division, does this space belong to?
o: The cranial cavity, part of the ventral cavity
The mediastinum, part of the thoracic cavity
The pelvic cavity, part of the ventral cavity
The vertebral cavity, part of the dorsal cavity
w: The spinal cord lies in the vertebral (spinal) cavity. Together with the cranial cavity, it forms the dorsal body cavity, protected by bone and meninges.

n.0: The cranial cavity holds the brain, and it belongs to the dorsal cavity, not the ventral cavity.
n.1: The mediastinum is in the ventral thoracic cavity and holds the heart, trachea and esophagus, not the spinal cord.
n.2: The pelvic cavity holds the bladder, rectum and reproductive organs; the spinal cord lies in the dorsal cavity.

q: In the nine-region scheme of the abdomen, three regions run down the midline. Which region lies directly inferior to the umbilical region?
o: Right lumbar region
Hypogastric (pubic) region
Epigastric region
Left iliac (inguinal) region
w: The middle column of the nine regions runs epigastric (top), umbilical (middle), hypogastric or pubic (bottom). The hypogastric region lies directly below the umbilical region.

n.0: The right lumbar region lies lateral to the umbilical region, in the middle row.
n.2: The epigastric region lies directly superior to the umbilical region, not inferior to it.
n.3: The left iliac (inguinal) region is in the bottom row but lateral, not directly below the umbilical region.

q: A patient points to an area of the abdomen directly beside the navel on their own right side. Using the nine-region scheme, which region is this?
o: Left lumbar region
Right iliac (inguinal) region
Right lumbar region
Right hypochondriac region
w: The middle row of the nine regions runs right lumbar, umbilical, left lumbar. The area beside the navel on the patient's own right is the right lumbar region.

n.0: Regions are named for the patient's own sides, so the patient's right side is the right lumbar region.
n.1: The right iliac (inguinal) region is in the bottom row, below the right lumbar region.
n.3: The right hypochondriac region is in the top row, beneath the lower ribs, above the right lumbar region.

q: A patient's chart notes a rash in the popliteal region and on the plantar surface of the same leg. Which two areas are affected?
o: The front of the thigh and the sole of the foot
The front of the knee and the sole of the foot
The back of the knee and the sole of the foot
The back of the knee and the top of the foot
w: Two regional terms: popliteal means the back of the knee, and plantar means the sole of the foot.

n.0: The front of the thigh is part of the femoral region; popliteal is the back of the knee.
n.1: The front of the knee is the patellar region; popliteal is the back of the knee.
n.3: Popliteal is right, but plantar is the sole, not the top of the foot.

q: The cardiologist examined the pericardium for signs of infection after the patient's chest surgery. Based on its prefix, where is the pericardium located?
o: Around the heart
Beside the heart
Within the heart
Below the heart
w: peri- means around and cardi/o means heart, so the pericardium is the sac that surrounds the heart.

n.1: Beside is a meaning of para-, the look-alike prefix; peri- means around.
n.2: Within would use endo- or intra- (the endocardium lines the inside of the heart).
n.3: Below would use sub- or hypo-, not peri-.

q: The suprarenal glands are named for where they sit. Based on its word parts, the term suprarenal describes a location
o: within the kidneys
above the liver
above the kidneys
below the kidneys
w: supra- means above and ren/o means kidney, so suprarenal means above the kidney. The suprarenal (adrenal) glands sit on top of the kidneys.

n.0: Within would use intra- (intrarenal); supra- means above.
n.1: The liver is hepat/o; ren/o means kidney.
n.3: Below would use sub- or infra-; supra- means above.

q: Using word parts, which term names the connective tissue membrane that wraps the outer surface of a bone?
o: Epimysium
Endosteum
Perichondrium
Periosteum
w: peri- means around and oste/o means bone, so the periosteum is the membrane around the outside of a bone. It anchors tendons and ligaments and carries the bone's vessels and nerves.

n.0: epi- means upon and my/o means muscle: the epimysium wraps a whole muscle, not a bone.
n.1: endo- means within: the endosteum lines the inner marrow cavity of a bone, not its outer surface.
n.2: peri- is right, but chondr/o means cartilage: the perichondrium surrounds cartilage, not bone.

q: After a fall from a ladder, a construction worker had a CT scan that ruled out intracranial bleeding. Based on its word parts, where would intracranial bleeding occur?
o: Between the skull bones
Around the outer skull
Below the skull
Inside the skull
w: intra- means within and crani/o means skull, so intracranial means inside the skull.

n.0: Between is inter-, the look-alike prefix.
n.1: Around is peri- or circum-.
n.2: Below is sub- or hypo-.

q: The intercostal muscles help lift the rib cage during breathing. Based on the word parts, where are these muscles located?
o: Beneath the ribs
Between the vertebrae
Between the ribs
Within the rib bones
w: inter- means between and cost/o means rib, so the intercostal muscles lie in the spaces between adjacent ribs.

n.0: Beneath would use sub- (subcostal); inter- means between.
n.1: The vertebrae use the root vertebr/o; cost/o means rib.
n.3: Within would use intra-; these muscles span the spaces between ribs, not the inside of the bones.

q: The subclavian artery carries blood toward the arm. Based on its word parts, where does this artery run?
o: Beside the sternum
Beneath the clavicle
Above the clavicle
Beneath the scapula
w: sub- means below or beneath, and the clavicle is the collarbone, so the subclavian artery runs beneath the clavicle on its way to the arm.

n.0: Beside the sternum would be parasternal; the term is built on the clavicle.
n.2: Above the clavicle would be supraclavicular (supra- above); sub- means beneath.
n.3: Beneath the scapula (shoulder blade) would be subscapular; the root here is clavicle.

q: The right and left hypochondriac regions are two of the nine abdominal regions. Based on the word parts, where do they lie?
o: Above the stomach region
Below the rib cartilages
Below the umbilical region
Beside the hip bones
w: hypo- means below and chondr/o means cartilage, so the hypochondriac regions lie below the costal cartilages of the lower ribs, at the two sides of the top row of the nine regions.

n.0: Above the stomach describes the epigastric region (epi- upon, gastr/o stomach), the middle of the top row.
n.2: The region below the umbilical region is the hypogastric (pubic) region, the middle of the bottom row.
n.3: The regions beside the hip bones are the iliac (inguinal) regions of the bottom row.

q: Bone is constantly remodeled. Based on the word parts, which bone cell breaks down bone matrix and releases calcium into the blood?
o: Osteoclast
Chondroblast
Osteocyte
Osteoblast
w: oste/o means bone and -clast means breaker, so osteoclasts break down (resorb) bone matrix, releasing calcium.

n.1: chondr/o means cartilage: chondroblasts build cartilage matrix.
n.2: -cyte means cell: osteocytes are mature bone cells that maintain the matrix around them.
n.3: -blast means builder: osteoblasts lay down new bone matrix.

q: Insulin is often injected into the hypodermis. Based on its word parts, where is this layer located?
o: Within the dermis
Beneath the dermis
Around the dermis
Above the dermis
w: hypo- means below and derm/o means skin, so the hypodermis (subcutaneous layer) lies beneath the dermis.

n.0: Within the dermis would be intradermal (intra- within).
n.2: Around would use peri-; the hypodermis is a layer below the dermis, not a wrapping.
n.3: The layer above the dermis is the epidermis (epi- upon).

q: During a shoulder exam, a patient is asked to abduct her arm. Based on its prefix, which movement is requested?
o: Moving the arm toward the midline
Moving the arm away from the midline
Turning the arm around its long axis
Bending the arm forward at the shoulder
w: ab- means away from, so abduction moves a limb away from the midline of the body, as when the arm is raised out to the side.

n.0: Moving toward the midline is adduction (ad- toward), the look-alike term.
n.2: Turning a limb around its long axis is rotation.
n.3: Bending the arm forward at the shoulder is flexion.

q: A physiology instructor asks the class to define homeostasis in a single sentence. Which statement best defines homeostasis?
o: Keeping each internal variable fixed at one exact, unchanging value
Adjusting the internal environment to match conditions outside the body
Maintaining a relatively stable internal environment as conditions change
Amplifying a change in the body until a specific end event is reached
w: Homeostasis is the maintenance of a relatively stable internal environment. Variables fluctuate within a narrow range around a set point rather than staying fixed.

n.0: Homeostasis is dynamic: variables such as body temperature move within a narrow range around a set point rather than holding one exact value.
n.1: Homeostasis keeps the internal environment stable despite outside changes; it does not make it match the outside.
n.3: Amplifying a change until an end event describes positive feedback, which is one mechanism, not the definition of homeostasis.

q: A feedback loop has three main components. Which component receives information about a change and compares it with the set point before directing a response?
o: Effector
Stimulus
Sensory receptor
Control center
w: The receptor (sensor) detects the change, the control center (often the brain, such as the hypothalamus) compares it with the set point, and the effector (a muscle or gland) produces the response.

n.0: The effector, a muscle or gland, carries out the response that the control center directs.
n.1: The stimulus is the change itself, not a component that processes information.
n.2: The receptor detects the change and sends the information on; it does not compare it with the set point.

q: Most homeostatic mechanisms use negative feedback, but a few use positive feedback. Which of the following is an example of positive feedback?
o: Oxytocin release that strengthens uterine contractions in labor
A slower heart rate that lowers a sudden rise in blood pressure
Insulin release that lowers blood glucose after a meal
Shivering that raises body temperature when it falls
w: During childbirth, pressure on the cervix triggers oxytocin release, which strengthens contractions, which triggers more oxytocin. The change is amplified until the baby is delivered.

n.1: The baroreceptor reflex reverses a rise in blood pressure, which is negative feedback.
n.2: Insulin reverses a rise in blood glucose, which is negative feedback.
n.3: Shivering reverses a fall in body temperature, which is negative feedback.

q: During a long run on a hot day, a runner's sweat glands release sweat, and its evaporation cools the skin. In this feedback loop, which role do the sweat glands play?
o: Control center
Receptor
Effector
Set point
w: An effector is the muscle or gland that produces the response. The sweat glands carry out the cooling response directed by the control center (the hypothalamus).

n.0: The control center for body temperature is the hypothalamus in the brain, which directs the sweat glands.
n.1: Receptors are the temperature sensors that detect the rise; the sweat glands respond to the change.
n.3: The set point is the target value (normal body temperature), not a structure.

q: After a large meal, blood glucose rises, the pancreas releases insulin, and blood glucose falls back to normal. Why is this classified as negative feedback?
o: The response lowers a variable, and any decrease counts as negative feedback
The response amplifies the rise until all of the glucose has been stored
The control center is a gland rather than the brain, which defines negative feedback
The response reverses the original change, bringing glucose back toward normal
w: Negative feedback means the response opposes (reverses) the original change. A rise in glucose leads to a response that lowers it back toward the set point.

n.0: "Negative" refers to opposing the change, not to lowering a value. Releasing glucagon to raise low blood glucose is also negative feedback.
n.1: Amplifying a change describes positive feedback. Insulin opposes the rise in glucose.
n.2: Feedback type depends on whether the response opposes or amplifies the change, not on which structure acts as the control center.

q: In the baroreceptor reflex that corrects a sudden rise in blood pressure, where are the receptors, and which brain region is the control center?
o: Carotid and aortic bodies; medulla oblongata
Carotid sinus and aortic arch; hypothalamus
Carotid sinus and aortic arch; medulla oblongata
Carotid and aortic bodies; hypothalamus
w: Baroreceptors (stretch receptors) in the carotid sinus and the aortic arch detect the rise in pressure and signal the medulla oblongata, which slows the heart and dilates vessels. The response reverses the change: negative feedback.

n.0: The medulla is the right control center, but the carotid and aortic bodies hold chemoreceptors that sense O2, CO2 and H+, not pressure.
n.1: The receptor sites are right, but blood pressure reflexes run through the medulla; the hypothalamus is the control center for temperature and water balance.
n.3: The carotid and aortic bodies are chemoreceptor sites, and the hypothalamus is not the control center for the baroreceptor reflex.

q: When blood pressure suddenly rises, stretch receptors in large arteries signal the brain, which then slows the heart rate. Which statement correctly identifies the type of feedback and the heart's role?
o: Positive feedback; the heart acts as the effector
Negative feedback; the heart acts as the receptor
Negative feedback; the heart acts as the effector
Positive feedback; the heart acts as the control center
w: Two steps. Slowing the heart reverses the rise in pressure, so this is negative feedback (the baroreceptor reflex). The heart carries out the response directed by the brain, so it is the effector.

n.0: The heart is the effector, but the response opposes the rise in blood pressure, which is negative feedback.
n.1: This is negative feedback, but the receptors are the stretch receptors in the arteries; the heart produces the response.
n.3: The response opposes the change (negative feedback), and the control center is the brain, not the heart.

q: When a vessel is cut, platelets that stick to the injury release chemicals that attract more platelets, and the process speeds up until the opening is sealed. Which statement best describes this process?
o: Negative feedback, because sealing the wound restores normal blood volume
Positive feedback, because each step intensifies the next until a clot forms
Positive feedback, because the outcome is helpful to the body's survival
Negative feedback, because platelet numbers return to their usual set point
w: Each platelet that sticks recruits more platelets, so the response amplifies the original change until an end event (the clot) stops it. Amplification toward an end event is positive feedback.

n.0: Restoring blood volume is the result of the sealed wound, not the mechanism: each platelet recruits more platelets, amplifying the change, so the loop is positive feedback.
n.2: This is positive feedback, but because the response amplifies the change, not because the outcome is helpful.
n.3: The process builds up platelets at the injury site rather than reversing a change back to a set point.

q: A swimmer's core temperature falls to 35 degrees C (95 degrees F) in cold water, and her skeletal muscles begin shivering. Which statement best describes the shivering?
o: A receptor response that detects the drop in core temperature
A positive feedback response that amplifies the temperature drop
A control center response that lowers the body's temperature set point
An effector response in negative feedback that generates heat
w: Skeletal muscles are effectors. Shivering produces heat that reverses the fall in temperature, so it is a negative feedback response.

n.0: Temperature receptors detect the drop; the shivering muscles produce the response.
n.1: Shivering opposes the drop by generating heat, so it does not amplify the change.
n.2: The control center (hypothalamus) directs shivering to restore the set point, not to lower it.

q: In an experiment, the receptors that monitor blood pressure in an animal are prevented from sending signals to the brain. Which outcome is most likely?
o: Blood pressure would stay at its set point, because no corrections occur
The effectors would amplify each change until an end event occurred
Changes would go undetected, so blood pressure would vary more widely
The control center would switch the loop over to positive feedback
w: Without receptor input, the control center cannot detect changes from the set point, so it cannot trigger corrective responses. Blood pressure would drift more widely than normal.

n.0: Corrections are what hold a variable near its set point; without them the variable drifts.
n.1: Amplification is a feature of positive feedback loops; losing receptors removes the signal that starts any correction.
n.3: Loss of receptor input does not turn a negative feedback loop into a positive one; the loop simply stops correcting.
